questions.prompt: One extended measurement update does which of the following?
questions.explanation: The nonlinear map \(h\) is replaced by \(h(\hat x) + J_h(\hat x)\,(x - \hat x)\). The innovation is the reading minus \(h(\hat x)\), and the gain uses \(J_h(\hat x)\) where a linear update would use the measurement row. A map with no derivative has no linear model to update. A frozen Jacobian ignores the move of the estimate. The prior variance enters the gain, not the innovation.

questions.prompt: A position estimate is \(3\), and the sensor reads the square of position. What is the measurement Jacobian at that estimate?
questions.explanation: The map is \(u^2\), so its derivative is \(2u\). At \(u = 3\) the Jacobian is \(6\). Reporting \(3\) uses the estimate in place of the derivative. Reporting \(9\) is the map \(3^2\), which belongs in the innovation, not in the gain as the Jacobian. Reporting \(2\) is the factor in \(2u\) with the estimate left out.

questions.prompt: The innovation of a sensor that reads \(u^2\), at an estimate of \(3\), with a reading of \(15\), is
questions.explanation: The innovation subtracts the nonlinear map at the estimate: \(3^2 = 9\), so \(15 - 9 = 6\). Subtracting the Jacobian \(6\) treats the derivative as if it were the predicted reading. Subtracting the estimate treats the sensor as the identity. The Jacobian enters the gain and the variance, not as a substitute for the predicted reading.

questions.prompt: Put one extended measurement update in order. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The map and the Jacobian are the linear model, so they come first. The innovation uses the map. The gain uses the Jacobian and the two variances, and it needs the innovation only when the correction is applied. The variance update uses that gain and the same Jacobian. Linearizing at the corrected point is the next block, not this one.

steps: Evaluate the nonlinear measurement and its Jacobian at the current estimate.
Form the innovation as the reading minus that measurement value.
Compute the gain from the Jacobian, the estimate variance, and the measurement variance.
Add the gain times the innovation, and update the variance with the same Jacobian.

questions.prompt: Which statements about an extended measurement update hold?
questions.explanation:
The linear model is the map plus the Jacobian times the displacement, so the innovation subtracts the map, and the Jacobian is taken where the model was built.
• An affine map has a constant Jacobian, and the map minus that Jacobian times the estimate is the linear residual. The update is then the ordinary linear one.
• For the square sensor at estimate \(3\), prior variance \(1\), reading \(15\), and measurement variance \(12\), the update lands at \(3.75\). The derivative of the true nonlinear cost \(\tfrac12(u-3)^2 + \tfrac1{24}(15-u^2)^2\) there is \(21/128\), not zero, so the nonlinear cost is not minimized.
• The Jacobian of \(u^2\) at \(3.75\) is \(7.5\), not the \(6\) used for the step. The next block has to be linearized again.

questions.prompt: The prior variance is \(p\), the measurement Jacobian is \(j\), and the measurement variance is \(r\). The extended gain equals
questions.explanation: The Jacobian takes the place of the measurement row. The gain is \(p j / (j^2 p + r)\). Every name appears. Using the reading in place of \(j\) would mix the innovation into the gain. Dropping \(j\) from the numerator is the linear gain only for a row equal to \(1\). Adding \(j\) instead of squaring it is the wrong innovation variance.

questions.prompt: A note updates a square-of-position sensor at the estimate \(3\), with prior variance \(1\), reading \(15\), and measurement variance \(12\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The map \(9\) and the innovation \(6\) are correct, and \(2u\) at \(3\) is \(6\). The innovation variance is \(6^2\cdot 1 + 12 = 48\), so the gain is \(6/48 = 1/8\). Using the estimate \(3\) as the Jacobian is the false step. That substitution builds the gain from the wrong linear model.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a column of two labels</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">p</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">q</text></svg>
steps: The map at \(3\) is \(9\), so the innovation for the reading \(15\) is \(6\).
The derivative of \(u^2\) is \(2u\), so the Jacobian at \(3\) is \(6\).
The gain may be computed with Jacobian \(3\), the estimate itself.
With Jacobian \(6\), prior variance \(1\), and measurement variance \(12\), the gain is \(6/48 = 1/8\).
reasons: The derivative of \(u^2\) is \(2u\), so the Jacobian at \(3\) is \(6\), not \(3\).
The innovation for the reading \(15\) is not \(6\).
With Jacobian \(6\) the gain is not \(1/8\).

questions.prompt: Estimate \(3\), prior variance \(1\), square sensor, reading \(15\), measurement variance \(12\). The gain is \(1/8\) and the innovation is \(6\). What is the updated position?
questions.explanation: The correction is the gain times the innovation: \(\tfrac18\cdot 6 = 0.75\). Added to the estimate, the position is \(3.75\). Reporting \(0.75\) stops at the correction. Reporting \(6\) is the innovation. Reporting \(15\) keeps the reading as if it were a position. The variance update is \(0.25\), which is a different quantity.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping upward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: The variance update \((1 - K J_h)P\) uses the measurement Jacobian. Replacing \(J_h\) by \(1\) is valid when
questions.explanation: The factor \(1\) is the derivative of the identity map. A sensor that reads position has that Jacobian, and the linear variance update \((1 - K)P\) is the special case. The square sensor has Jacobian \(2u\), which equals \(1\) only at \(u = 1/2\). A positive gain does not make the Jacobian equal \(1\). A zero innovation leaves the estimate unmoved and does not change which Jacobian the variance formula uses.

questions.prompt: Solving \(F(x) = 0\) by rebuilding a tangent at every new point is the same linearization idea as an extended update. That root iteration is
questions.explanation: Newton replaces \(F\) by \(F(x) + J_F(x)\, d\) and solves the linear equation for \(d\). An extended update does the same to a measurement map and then blends the result with the prior. A batch gradient sums block gradients at one point. A simplex pivot changes a basis. A predict step propagates a state; it does not solve a tangent equation for a root.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
options: a predict step that adds process noise
Newton's method for a nonlinear equation
a batch gradient with a constant step
a simplex pivot

questions.prompt: For the square sensor at estimate \(3\), with prior variance \(1\), gain \(1/8\), and Jacobian \(6\), what is the updated variance?
questions.explanation: The variance update is \((1 - K J_h)P = (1 - \tfrac18\cdot 6)\cdot 1 = 1 - 0.75 = 0.25\). Using \((1 - K)P = 7/8\) pretends the Jacobian is \(1\). Reporting \(1\) keeps the prior variance. Reporting \(0.75\) is the amount removed, not the variance that remains.

questions.prompt: A Newton root iteration and an extended measurement update share which sensitivity?
questions.explanation: The next point is where the tangent hits the target. If the tangent is a poor picture of the map, that hit can sit far from a root. Neither method finishes a general nonlinear equation in one step: the square sensor's update at \(3.75\) is not a root of the nonlinear stationarity condition. Both methods use the derivative. The measurement variance shapes the gain of the filter update; Newton's method for a root has no measurement variance.
